name: Integration
summary: How Claude connects to the systems around it: MCP servers, APIs, tools, other agents and retrieval (RAG). Permissions, secrets, and what happens when an integration fails.
keyIdeas: Wrap a shared system once as an MCP server; many assistants reuse it.
Secrets live in the tool/server layer (env, secret manager), never in model context.
Least privilege: separate read tools from write/destructive tools; scope credentials per server.
Tool failures return structured errors (is_error) so the model can retry or report honestly.
Validate tool inputs server-side; tighten JSON schemas with enums, formats and examples.
stdio = local process; Streamable HTTP + auth = shared remote server.
RAG quality is usually a retrieval problem: metadata, versioning, filtering, chunking.
Subagents return compact structured summaries, not full transcripts.
traps: Putting credentials in the system prompt or tool descriptions.
Relying on a tool description sentence ('never call delete unless sure') as a security control.
Fixing bad RAG answers by stuffing more chunks into context.
Swallowing tool errors and returning empty 'success'.

name: Solution Design & Architecture
summary: Turning a business need into the right Claude design: single call vs fixed workflow vs agent vs multi-agent, plus batch vs real-time and where hard rules are enforced.
keyIdeas: Pick the simplest pattern that meets the requirement: call → workflow → agent → multi-agent.
Workflows (chaining, routing, parallelization) fit known, repeatable steps.
Agents fit open-ended tasks where steps can't be known in advance; give budgets and stop criteria.
Multi-agent pays off for parallelizable, independent subtasks needing separate contexts.
Batch processing for large, non-urgent volume; real-time for interactive latency.
Business rules (limits, approvals) are enforced in code, not in prompts.
A document that fits in context may not need RAG at all — consider long context + caching.
traps: Choosing an agent when a workflow solves it.
Multi-agent 'because it's important'.
Building a vector DB before checking whether the corpus fits in context.
Enforcing money/safety limits with a system prompt line.

name: Evaluation, Testing & Optimization
summary: Proving the system works before and after launch: success criteria, eval sets, code graders, LLM-as-judge, human review, slicing, regression testing and diagnosing failures.
keyIdeas: Success criteria and a representative eval set come before building.
Use the cheapest reliable grader: code grader > LLM-as-judge > human, by task.
Calibrate LLM judges against human labels; use specific rubrics.
Slice results by category; a better average can hide a critical regression.
Separate retrieval metrics (recall@k) from generation metrics (faithfulness).
Production monitoring feeds failures back into the eval set.
Optimize cost with caching, model routing and batching — then re-run evals.
traps: Shipping because the average score went up.
Trusting an uncalibrated LLM judge.
Swapping models before locating whether retrieval or generation failed.
Treating evals as a one-time pre-launch activity.

name: Governance, Safety & Risk Management
summary: Where guardrails belong, where humans review, data access and minimization, prompt injection, incident handling and compliance (GDPR, HIPAA, local data protection law).
keyIdeas: Compliance needs real controls in the system; a prompt line is not a control.
Data minimization: don't put data in context that the bot must never reveal.
Treat retrieved/inbound content as untrusted data (prompt injection).
Human-in-the-loop before irreversible or high-impact actions.
Enforce access control at retrieval time (document-level ACLs).
Audit logs: prompts, tool calls, approvals, identity — with redaction of sensitive data.
Incident response: contain, preserve evidence, notify, root-cause, add to evals.
Know where personal data lives (logs, vector stores, caches) so it can be deleted.
traps: 'Tell the model not to log PHI.'
Asking the model to check user permissions.
Human review on everything (or nothing) instead of risk-tiered review.
Deleting logs after an incident.

name: Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management
summary: The consulting side: discovery, expectations, explaining trade-offs in business terms, success metrics, change control, rollout, model upgrades and handoff.
keyIdeas: Discovery first: problem, users, current process, metrics, constraints, volume.
Reset '100% accurate' expectations into measurable targets plus error handling.
Explain model choice in business terms: quality bar met, cost, latency, scale.
Risk-tiered proposals resolve compliance-vs-automation conflicts.
Version prompts/configs; regression evals before every change.
Staged rollout, monitoring and a rollback plan.
Model upgrades go through the eval suite and a canary.
Handoff = runbook, evals, dashboards, incident path, ownership.
traps: Building before success criteria are agreed.
Promising perfection.
Editing production prompts live.
Switching to a new model the day it launches.

name: Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering
summary: Choosing the right model for capability, cost and speed; prompting techniques; structured output; prompt caching; and managing what goes into the context window.
keyIdeas: Small/fast model for high volume and tight latency; top model for hard reasoning and agentic coding.
Route: cheap model by default, escalate hard cases.
Long documents at the top, the question/instructions at the end.
XML tags, few-shot examples and tool schemas for consistent structure.
Let the model reason (extended thinking / step-by-step) for multi-step problems.
Prompt caching needs an identical prefix within the TTL.
System prompt = stable role/rules; user turn = per-request data.
Long sessions: compact history, trim stale tool output, store artifacts externally.
traps: Using the biggest model for everything.
Putting variable content before the cache breakpoint.
Fixing format problems by raising temperature.
Letting context fill with old tool output.

name: Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement
summary: How teams work with Claude day to day: Claude Code project settings, CLAUDE.md, permissions, MCP config, CI usage, reusable commands and rollout.
keyIdeas: Project CLAUDE.md is committed and shared; it holds conventions and commands.
.claude/settings.json is shared; .claude/settings.local.json is personal and not committed.
Deny rules and hooks block dangerous commands deterministically.
CI: least privilege, allowlisted tools, no production secrets, PR review.
Vetted MCP servers in project .mcp.json with scoped tokens.
Repeated workflows become custom commands/skills.
Pilot + training + managed policy settings for org rollout; measure outcomes.
traps: Sharing one API key in chat.
Letting everyone install arbitrary MCP servers.
Relying on a CLAUDE.md note to prevent destructive commands.
Measuring rollout by seat count.
